The Screaming piha (Lipaugus vociferans) is a Neotropical suboscine passerine renowned for its remarkably powerful vocalizations, which dominate the soundscape of Amazonian terra firme forests. As a frugivorous member of the Cotingidae family, its life history exhibits several characteristic adaptations tied to a relatively slow pace of life. Field studies indicate that freshly laid eggs, incubated at a mean nest temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a developmental duration consistent with that of other medium-bodied cotingids. Neonates emerge at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet body mass of just 7.9 grams [Ww0 = 7.9 grams] for the newly hatched chick, a value that underscores the altricial state of the young. This modest starting mass necessitates an extended period of intense parental provisioning within the nest. The nestling phase culminates in fledging, which has been documented to occur roughly 17 days after hatching [tx = roughly 17 days after hatching] when ambient conditions approach the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a thermal benchmark that appears to facilitate rapid feather development and neuromuscular coordination required for first flight.

Following the fledging event, juveniles enter a protracted period of somatic growth and social learning before reaching reproductive maturity. The attainment of puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, has been estimated at approximately 51 days after hatching [tp = approximately 51 days after hatching] under the warm thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterizes the piha's active metabolic state. However, despite the relatively early physiological capacity for reproduction, first successful breeding is typically deferred considerably. Data from long-term field observations suggest that individuals do not initiate their first brood until roughly 511 days after hatching [tR = roughly 511 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the time required to establish a territory, acquire sufficient foraging proficiency, and accumulate the body condition necessary to support the energetic demands of nesting at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This postponement of first reproduction is a common pattern among frugivorous canopy birds, where resource predictability and social competition are key constraints.

The ultimate body size attained by adult females is a critical determinant of reproductive output and survival. Adult females of Lipaugus vociferans reach a maximum recorded wet body mass of 75.4 grams [Wwi = 75.4 grams], placing them among the larger-bodied members of the genus. This asymptotic mass is achieved through a gradual growth trajectory that extends well beyond the fledging period, with young birds continuing to add mass for several months after leaving the nest. Body condition in females is tightly linked to clutch dynamics, as the energy reserves needed for egg formation and the subsequent demands of incubation are considerable for a species with a relatively high mass-specific metabolic rate. The energetic cost of maintaining this adult body mass is reflected in the species' basal metabolic rate, which has been quantified through respirometry. Under standard conditions at the species' typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum measured resting oxygen consumption reaches 138.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 138.18 milliliters per hour], a rate consistent with the elevated metabolic demands of a large, actively foraging frugivore in a warm, humid environment.

Reproductive output in the Screaming piha is characterized by a modest annual investment, consistent with a K-selected life-history strategy typical of many tropical forest birds. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a highly conservative clutch size that is common among cotingids and likely represents an adaptation to the challenges of provisioning a single, rapidly growing nestling in a resource-variable environment. Furthermore, breeding events are not continuous throughout the year; field records indicate that females typically initiate approximately 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches annually], with the breeding season timed to coincide with peak fruit abundance. This low reproductive rate, combining a clutch of one egg with a limited number of nesting attempts per year, results in a modest annual fecundity that is balanced by relatively high adult survival. The pace of this life history is further reflected in the species' maximum recorded longevity, with the oldest documented individual reaching an estimated lifespan of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under the warm thermal conditions typical of its habitat at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a duration that underscores the species' capacity for extended reproductive tenure.

Comparative physiological studies across the Cotingidae reveal that the metabolic and life-history traits of Lipaugus vociferans occupy a distinctive position within the family. The maximum resting metabolic rate of 138.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 138.18 milliliters per hour] measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is among the highest recorded for cotingids of its body size, a finding that aligns with the species' highly active, far-ranging foraging behavior and its need to sustain powerful vocal displays that can carry for over a kilometer through dense forest. This elevated metabolism necessitates a correspondingly high food intake, and the adult female mass of 75.4 grams [Wwi = 75.4 grams] is supported by a diet dominated by lipid-rich palm fruits and large arthropods. The developmental milestones, including a 16-day incubation at 37 °C [T = 37 °C] and a nestling phase extending to roughly 17 days after hatching [tx = roughly 17 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], culminate in a first reproduction event that is deferred to roughly 511 days after hatching [tR = roughly 511 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C, creating a life cycle where early mortality risks are high but adult survival is correspondingly high — a classic signature of a slow life-history strategy in a stable tropical environment.
